passage:
Note from the school nurse, Wednesday

Maria, age nine, fell from the climbing frame at lunch and landed on her left wrist. It was swollen and she was crying hard. I kept her still and comfortable and called her mother, who took her to the hospital. The X-ray showed a small fracture.
She came back today with a cast, angry that she cannot run in Sports Day. She asked me, "Will my hand ever work properly again?" I told her honestly that the doctor expects it to heal, and that bones take time.
We made a small plan together: she will be the official scorekeeper for her house and practise writing her name with her right hand. By home time she had written it three times and shown everyone.

Sharmila

qa.q: Where did Maria fall from?
qa.a: She fell from the climbing frame at lunch.

qa.q: What was Maria worried about when she spoke to Sharmila?
qa.a: She was scared her hand would never work properly again, and angry about missing Sports Day.

qa.q: How did Sharmila help Maria's mind heal along with her wrist?
qa.a: Sharmila gave honest information about healing and set small goals like scorekeeping and writing with her right hand.

qa.q: How might Maria's classmates see her as the official scorekeeper?
qa.a: They would likely see her as still part of Sports Day, and cheer her on as she practises writing with her right hand.

grounding: It shows a child hurt in play who is scared and angry about being stopped from playing, helped by comfort, honest information and small goals.

passage:
Saturday

Today I fell off my cycle near the park and hurt my ankle really badly. It went purple. At the hospital they put it in a hard boot and gave me crutches. Now I can't go to swimming for ages and the gala is soon. I cried and threw my pillow.
I asked Yamini Didi if I'll be slow forever. She sat on my bed and said, "Silly girl, the doctor said it will heal. It just takes its time."
Then she made me a chart with stars. Today's goal: walk to the window on crutches. I did it twice!
Tomorrow's goal: go to the balcony.
I'm still cross. But a bit less.

Nikita

qa.q: What did the hospital put on Nikita's ankle?
qa.a: They put it in a hard boot and gave her crutches.

qa.q: How was Nikita feeling about missing swimming?
qa.a: She felt angry and upset, crying and throwing her pillow, and worried about being slow forever.

qa.q: What small steps did Yamini Didi suggest, and why do they help?
qa.a: A star chart with small goals like walking to the window, because reaching them gives Nikita a sense of progress while the ankle heals.

qa.q: How might Yamini Didi feel seeing Nikita so upset?
qa.a: She probably feels sorry for her little sister and wants to calm her with honest words and a plan.

grounding: It shows a child hurt in a fall who is angry and scared about the future, helped by honest information and small achievable goals.

passage: Sumit, beta, stop scowling at that cast. Come sit with your Kamal Dada. When I was nine, in our village, I climbed the tallest mango tree and fell straight out of it. Snap went my arm. I screamed so loud the goats ran. I was frightened, and then I was angry, because it was kabaddi season and I was the best raider. I thought my arm would never be the same. My father sat with me that night. He didn't say 'stop crying'. He told me straight: 'Six weeks in the cast, then it will be weak, then it will get strong.' And every week he gave me a small job: carry the milk tin with my good hand, then squeeze a rubber ball. By the next season, I was raiding again. So, one week at a time, eh?

qa.q: What did young Kamal fall out of?
qa.a: The tallest mango tree.

qa.q: What was young Kamal feeling after breaking his arm?
qa.a: He was frightened, then angry about missing kabaddi season and worried his arm would never be the same.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Kamal's story?
qa.a: His father's honest explanation of how healing would go, and the small weekly jobs that gave him goals.

qa.q: How might Kamal's father have felt sitting with him that night?
qa.a: He was probably worried for his son but calm, wanting to give him honesty and hope.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a child who breaks an arm feeling scared, angry and worried, and how comfort, honest information and small goals help him heal.

passage: Zubin, ten, broke his ankle in a monsoon football match, slipping on the mud, and the doctor put it in a cast for six weeks. Sports day was next Friday, and Zubin was supposed to run the relay. Worse, their building in Mumbai had no lift, and they lived on the fourth floor. He cried with rage. 'I'll miss everything! And what if I can never run again?' His father Saurabh sat on the edge of the bed. 'I'm sorry, Zubin. It's rotten luck. The doctor said the bone heals in six weeks, then your leg needs a few more weeks to get strong. You will run again.' Zubin sniffed. 'But sports day…' 'Could you be team captain from the sideline? And this week, let's aim for hopping to the balcony with the crutches.' By Thursday, Zubin could hop there and back.

qa.q: What floor does Zubin's family live on?
qa.a: The fourth floor.

qa.q: What was Zubin worried about besides missing sports day?
qa.a: He was afraid that he might never run again.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do to help Zubin's mind heal?
qa.a: He comforted him, gave honest information about healing, and set small achievable goals like captaining from the sideline and hopping to the balcony.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt watching Zubin cry with rage?
qa.a: He probably felt sorry and sad for his son, but steady enough to help.

grounding: Shows a child injured in play who is scared and angry at missing out, and how comfort, honest information and small goals help his mind heal.

passage: Shankar, eight, had fallen off his cycle racing down the slope in their Coimbatore colony. Now his knee had six stitches and his wrist was in a bandage. He sat on the sofa, arms folded. 'I'm never cycling again,' he said, though his eyes kept going to the cycle by the door. His older brother Chaitanya sat beside him with a bowl of peanuts. 'That was a big fall. Were you scared?' Shankar's lip trembled. 'Yes. And now I can't play for ages.' 'The doctor said two weeks for the stitches. Then you can try again on the flat part first.' Chaitanya handed him a peanut. 'Today's goal: walk to the gate and back.' Shankar did it, limping. The next day, he walked to the park. By the end of the week, he was asking about the cycle.

qa.q: How many stitches did Shankar's knee have?
qa.a: Six stitches.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling as he sat with arms folded?
qa.a: He was scared after the fall and angry that he could not play, saying he would never cycle again.

qa.q: What small goals did Chaitanya set?
qa.a: Walking to the gate and back, then trying cycling on the flat part first when healed.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt when Shankar asked about the cycle again?
qa.a: He was probably relieved and pleased to see his brother's confidence coming back.

grounding: Shows a child hurt in a fall feeling scared and angry at being stopped from playing, and how comfort, honest information and small goals help him recover.

passage:
"The plaster stays on till after the race?" Damini stared at her arm. "The inter-school race is so soon!"
"I know," said Papa Lokesh, sitting on the edge of her bed. "It's rotten luck."
"It's not luck, it's that stupid swing. I hate it." Her lip shook. "Will my arm be bent forever?"
"The doctor showed us the X-ray, remember? The bone is in a straight line. It will knit back."
"But I'll be slow when I come back. Everyone will beat me."
"Maybe at first. So let's make small goals. This week, you learn to write your name with your left hand."
"That's silly."
"Is it? Bet you can't do it."
Damini narrowed her eyes, grabbed a pencil and started. "Watch me."

qa.q: What small goal does Papa suggest for this week?
qa.a: Learning to write her name with her left hand.

qa.q: What was Damini worried about, apart from missing the race?
qa.a: She was scared her arm would stay bent and worried that everyone would beat her when she came back.

qa.q: Which parts of Papa's response help Damini's mind heal too?
qa.a: He agrees it's rotten luck, gives honest information from the X-ray, and turns her energy to a small goal she can achieve.

qa.q: How might Papa Lokesh feel seeing Damini's lip shake?
qa.a: He probably feels sad for her and protective, which is why he stays calm and turns it into a playful challenge.

grounding: Shows a child with a broken arm feeling angry, scared and worried about the future, and comfort, honest information and a small goal helping her mind heal.
